title: Saw Point | Issue 003
excerpt: September’s timber market showed firmer order books, steady China log demand and growing interest from India, while mill closures and rising fuel costs continue to reshape supply and pricing across New Zealand. This edition also looks at pressure on local processors and the case for more investment in value-added wood processing.
body:
There are some better signs coming out of the timber market. Order books appear to be improving and we're seeing some upward pressure on pricing.

At the same time, New Zealand has lost more sawmilling capacity.

When a mill closes, the customers it was supplying don't necessarily disappear. Those orders have to be picked up elsewhere.

So fuller order books and firmer pricing aren't necessarily just about demand improving. Fewer mills supplying the market is likely playing a part as well.

Sources: Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, September 2026; PF Olsen / Stand Forestry: Log Market, July 2026


MARKET UPDATE: CHINA CONTINUES TO HOLD STEADY
September was another relatively steady month for the China log market.

A-grade settlements were around USD 130 per JASm³, daily softwood usage remained around 55,000 to 60,000 m³ and inventory was approximately 2.4 million m³.

After the volatility we've seen in export markets over the years, there's something to be said for boring.

Logs are moving through the ports and inventory remains manageable. The challenge is still at the New Zealand end, where freight and distance from port continue to put pressure on forest returns.

China's Golden Week will affect October consumption and inventory numbers, so the next set of figures will need some context.

Source: Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, September 2026


EXPORT WATCH: INDIA HAS INTEREST, BUT PRICE IS STILL THE PROBLEM
India continues to come up as a potential growth market for New Zealand wood products.

WPMA reported more than 100 new business contacts from MumbaiWood across importers, manufacturers, architects and traders.

There's certainly no shortage of enquiry for sawn timber. The problem is converting it into business at workable price levels.

Price expectations are often below where New Zealand processors can realistically supply, particularly once freight is included.

Improved market access should help, but finding products and customers where New Zealand processors can compete and make a return remains the challenge.

Sources: WPMA: MumbaiWood 2026 – Business Opportunities and Challenges; Wood Central: Indian Importers ‘Mean Business’ on NZ Pine; Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, September 2026


ONE TO WATCH: COULD HIGHER FUEL COSTS BRING FAF BACK?
Fuel costs are back on the watch list.

The latest industry update we've received has fuel costs back above the supplier's FAF trigger level, with FAF being considered again if prices remain elevated at the next review.

For timber, diesel matters. Logs and finished products move considerable distances and higher transport costs flow directly into the delivered price.

FAF hasn't been widely talked about for a while, but if diesel remains elevated it could start appearing again in parts of the market.

Sources: MBIE: Weekly Fuel Price Monitoring; *industry supplier update


SAW POINT
New Zealand's secondary wood processors are under pressure.

For years, New Zealand has exported large volumes of radiata logs to China, where timber is processed at enormous scale. At the same time, manufactured wood products are imported into New Zealand, with some competing at price points that are difficult for local processors to match.

The answer isn't to blame imports or stop exporting logs. It's worth looking at why China can make the economics work.

Scale, manufacturing efficiency, logistics and access to large markets all play a part. New Zealand won't replicate China, but there are lessons in where we invest and which products we choose to manufacture here.

There's another change happening at home. As secondary processors close or become part of vertically integrated businesses, established supply channels change. Product that once moved through one processor or customer can be absorbed into another supply chain, leaving others looking for new markets.

The effect also runs back into the forest.

Pruning is a good example. If the clearwood premium doesn't justify the additional cost, there is less incentive for forest owners to prune. In tighter years, some growers may choose not to undertake a pruning regime at all.

More investment in competitive processing and engineered wood products would give New Zealand more ways to add value to the resource here, particularly in forestry-dependent regions.

We don't need to process every log in New Zealand. Log exports remain an important part of the industry.

But retaining the ability to process and add value to our own resource matters too.

Sources: MPI: Forestry and Wood Processing Data; MPI: Wood Product Markets Data; PF Olsen / Stand Forestry: Log Market, July 2026; MPI: Wood Processing Growth Fund

MPI's latest public trade data includes June 2026 quarterly imports and exports, while PF Olsen's July 2026 report directly states that recent mill closures have tightened domestic timber supply.


WORTH READING THIS MONTH
Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, September 2026

China pricing and inventory, freight, India and New Zealand processing conditions.

WPMA: MumbaiWood 2026

An update on the industry's work developing India as a market for New Zealand wood products.

Wood Central: Indian Importers ‘Mean Business’ on NZ Pine

More detail on Indian interest in New Zealand radiata and processed timber.

MPI: New Zealand Forestry and Wood Processing Data

Useful background on New Zealand's forestry exports and the balance between logs and processed wood products.

MPI: Wood Processing Growth Fund

Examples of investment supporting higher-value and onshore wood processing in New Zealand.


Saw Point is published monthly by FPX, Forest Products Exchange.

Written by George Harman | Founder, FPX | Director, Sutcliffe Trading
